column1: A pure compound contains elements in a definite chemical proportion.|T|Its composition follows its chemical formula rather than varying freely like a mixture.
Melting ice is a chemical reaction.|F|It changes water’s physical state without changing its chemical identity.
Density is an intensive property.|T|For a uniform material at fixed conditions, it does not depend on sample size.
Mass is an extensive property.|T|Combining samples adds their masses.
A homogeneous mixture has uniform composition at the scale considered.|T|Its components are distributed evenly rather than forming visibly distinct portions.
Significant figures express unlimited certainty in a measured value.|F|They reflect the precision supported by the measurement and include an uncertain final digit.
Exact counted quantities can limit a calculation’s significant figures just like uncertain measurements.|F|Exact counts do not introduce measurement uncertainty and do not limit significant figures.
A physical change necessarily creates a new chemical substance.|F|Changes of state and shape can preserve chemical identity.
Unit conversion factors represent ratios of equivalent quantities.|T|Multiplying by such a factor changes the units without changing the physical quantity.
An atom’s atomic number equals its number of protons.|T|The proton count determines which element it is.
Isotopes of an element have different numbers of protons.|F|Isotopes share proton count but differ in neutron count.
A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.|T|Their opposite electric charges balance.
A positive ion has lost electrons relative to the neutral atom.|T|Removing negative charge leaves a net positive charge.
Electrons contribute most of an atom’s mass.|F|Protons and neutrons contribute nearly all the mass.
An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number atom ratio.|T|It need not show the actual atom count in a molecule.
A molecular formula is always identical to its empirical formula.|F|For example, a molecule can contain a whole-number multiple of the simplest ratio.
Ionic compound formulas balance total positive and negative charge.|T|An ordinary bulk ionic compound is electrically neutral overall.
Average atomic mass accounts for naturally occurring isotope abundances.|T|It is an abundance-weighted average rather than a simple unweighted average.
Photon energy increases with frequency.|T|Energy is Planck’s constant times frequency.
An orbital is a classical electron path around the nucleus.|F|It is a quantum description of a spatial probability distribution.
Each orbital can hold at most two electrons with opposite spins.|T|The Pauli principle restricts electrons sharing the same spatial orbital.
Hund’s rule favors occupying degenerate orbitals singly before pairing.|T|The singly occupied orbitals have parallel spins in the lowest-energy arrangement.
Across a typical main-group period, atomic radius generally increases from left to right.|F|Increasing effective nuclear attraction generally makes radius decrease across the period.
Removing an electron from an isolated gaseous atom requires ionization energy.|T|The energy overcomes attraction between the electron and the remaining ion.
A principal quantum number can be zero for a bound atomic orbital.|F|Its allowed values begin at one.
The s subshell contains three orbitals.|F|It contains one orbital; a p subshell contains three.
An anion is generally larger than its neutral parent atom.|T|Extra electrons increase repulsion and reduce effective attraction per electron.
A covalent bond involves shared electron density between atoms.|T|The shared electrons can lower the energy of the bonded arrangement.
A polar covalent bond shares electrons equally.|F|Different electronegativities produce unequal sharing.
A molecule with polar bonds must always be polar overall.|F|Bond dipoles can cancel in a sufficiently symmetric geometry.
A lone pair can affect molecular shape.|T|Its electron density repels other electron groups around the central atom.
VSEPR predicts shape by considering repulsions between valence electron groups.|T|Groups arrange to reduce repulsion, including bonding and nonbonding groups.
A double bond counts as two separate directions in basic VSEPR electron-group counting.|F|Multiple bonds count as one electron group, though their repulsion can differ from a single bond.
Resonance structures differ in atom connectivity.|F|They describe the same atomic arrangement with different electron placements.
Formal charge equals the atom’s full measurable physical charge in every molecule.|F|It is a bookkeeping assignment, not generally the actual partial charge.
Breaking a chemical bond requires energy input.|T|Bond formation releases energy, while separating bonded atoms costs energy.
A sigma bond has electron density along the internuclear axis.|T|It can arise from end-to-end orbital overlap.
A pi bond is formed by sideways overlap of suitable orbitals.|T|Its electron density lies on opposite sides of the internuclear axis.
A carbon-carbon double bond consists of two sigma bonds.|F|It contains one sigma bond and one pi bond.
An sp-hybridized center is associated with a linear two-direction arrangement.|T|The two hybrid orbitals point oppositely, giving an ideal angle of 180 degrees.
An sp²-hybridized center has an ideal trigonal-planar arrangement.|T|Three hybrid directions lie in a plane at approximately 120 degrees.
Antibonding molecular-orbital occupancy generally weakens a bond.|T|It reduces bond order relative to filling bonding orbitals alone.
A molecule with unpaired electrons can be paramagnetic.|T|Unpaired electron magnetic moments can align with an applied field.
Bond order in simple molecular-orbital counting is bonding electrons minus antibonding electrons, divided by two.|T|A positive value indicates net bonding in that model.
Hybridization is a literal mechanical reshaping process visible before bonding.|F|It is a mathematical orbital model used to describe bonding geometry.
One mole contains Avogadro’s number of specified entities.|T|The entities may be atoms, molecules, ions, or other clearly identified particles.
Molar mass converts between mass and amount in moles.|T|Dividing mass by molar mass gives the number of moles.
Molarity is moles of solute per liter of solution.|T|The denominator is total solution volume, not solvent volume alone.
Diluting a solution with solvent increases its solute amount.|F|The amount of solute stays fixed unless solute is added or removed.
A dilution lowers concentration when solution volume increases and solute amount is unchanged.|T|The same amount is spread through a larger volume.
Mass percent is component mass divided by total sample mass, multiplied by 100.|T|It expresses the component’s share of the total mass.
An empirical formula can be determined from mole ratios of elements.|T|Convert each element’s amount to moles and reduce the ratios to whole numbers.
Two solutions with equal molarity must contain equal solute amounts regardless of volume.|F|Amount equals molarity times volume, so different volumes can contain different amounts.
A solution’s molarity can change with temperature because its volume can change.|T|The solute amount may remain fixed while thermal expansion alters the denominator.
Balancing a reaction changes coefficients rather than chemical subscripts.|T|Subscripts define substances; coefficients count the amounts reacting.
A balanced equation conserves the number of atoms of each element.|T|Chemical reactions rearrange atoms rather than creating or destroying them.
The limiting reactant is always the reactant with the smallest mass.|F|Compare available moles with the required stoichiometric ratios.
The theoretical yield is calculated from the limiting reactant.|T|That reactant sets the maximum product amount under complete ideal conversion.
Percent yield compares actual yield with theoretical yield.|T|Divide actual by theoretical and multiply by 100.
Oxidation involves a decrease in oxidation number.|F|Oxidation raises oxidation number and corresponds to electron loss in the accounting scheme.
A reducing agent is itself oxidized.|T|It supplies electrons to the species being reduced.
A net ionic equation omits spectator ions.|T|Only species undergoing the chemical change remain.
Stoichiometric mole ratios come from the balanced equation’s coefficients.|T|They relate reacting amounts, not directly their masses.
Gas-law temperatures should be expressed in kelvin.|T|Absolute temperature correctly represents the thermal scale in ideal-gas relationships.
At fixed amount and temperature, ideal-gas pressure is inversely proportional to volume.|T|Compressing the same gas increases its pressure in Boyle’s law.
At fixed pressure and amount, an ideal gas’s volume rises with absolute temperature.|T|Charles’s law makes volume proportional to kelvin temperature.
An ideal gas has substantial attractive interactions between its particles by assumption.|F|The ideal model neglects intermolecular interactions except elastic collisions.
The total pressure of an ideal-gas mixture is the sum of its partial pressures.|T|Each gas contributes according to its own amount and the shared volume and temperature.
At equal temperature, all gases have equal root-mean-square molecular speed.|F|Lighter particles move faster on average at the same temperature.
Effusion involves gas passing through a very small opening.|T|It differs from diffusion, which describes spreading and mixing through space.
Real-gas effects become important at high pressure and low temperature.|T|Finite molecular volume and attractive interactions then matter more.
The ideal-gas constant must have units compatible with the units used for pressure and volume.|T|Using a mismatched numerical constant produces an incorrect result even with correct algebra.
Heat flows spontaneously from a hotter object to a cooler object.|T|The direction reduces the temperature difference without external work.
An exothermic reaction releases heat to the surroundings.|T|At constant pressure its reaction enthalpy change is negative.
An endothermic reaction has a negative enthalpy change.|F|It absorbs heat and has positive reaction enthalpy at constant pressure.
Enthalpy is a state function.|T|Its change depends on the initial and final states, not the reaction path.
Reversing a reaction reverses the sign of its enthalpy change.|T|The same energy difference is traversed in the opposite direction.
Multiplying a reaction equation by two doubles its reaction enthalpy.|T|Enthalpy change is extensive and scales with reacting amount.
Hess’s law combines reaction steps by adding their enthalpy changes.|T|State-function behavior makes the sum independent of the chosen intermediate steps.
A calorimeter’s own heat capacity can always be ignored.|F|It can absorb appreciable heat and must be included when relevant or calibrated.
Breaking bonds releases energy while forming bonds consumes it.|F|Breaking bonds consumes energy; forming bonds releases it.
Intermolecular forces act between molecules.|T|They differ from the bonds holding atoms together within a molecule.
Dispersion forces occur only in polar molecules.|F|Temporary fluctuations create dispersion attractions even between nonpolar particles.
Hydrogen bonding can occur when suitable hydrogen donors interact with suitable lone-pair acceptors.|T|Common donors contain hydrogen bonded to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine.
Stronger intermolecular attractions generally raise boiling temperature among otherwise comparable substances.|T|More energy is needed to separate particles into the gas phase.
Evaporation occurs only at the boiling point.|F|Energetic surface molecules can escape at temperatures below boiling.
At dynamic vapor-liquid equilibrium, evaporation and condensation both stop.|F|Both continue at equal rates, keeping macroscopic amounts stable.
A liquid boils when its vapor pressure matches the external pressure.|T|Vapor bubbles can then form throughout the liquid rather than only at its surface.
A crystalline solid has a repeating long-range arrangement.|T|Its ordered structure distinguishes it from an amorphous solid.
The triple point represents coexistence of solid, liquid, and gas at specified conditions.|T|All three phases are in equilibrium there.
Dissolving a substance always raises the solution temperature.|F|Dissolution can release or absorb heat depending on interactions broken and formed.
Like dissolves like is a useful guide based on compatible intermolecular interactions.|T|It is a heuristic rather than a guarantee for every substance pair.
For many gases, solubility in a liquid increases with gas partial pressure at fixed temperature.|T|Henry’s law describes this proportionality in its applicable dilute regime.
Molality uses kilograms of solvent in its denominator.|T|It counts solute moles per solvent mass, unlike molarity’s solution-volume denominator.
Colligative properties depend primarily on the number of dissolved particles in the ideal dilute model.|T|Particle count matters more than chemical identity under the model’s assumptions.
A nonvolatile solute raises the solvent’s vapor pressure in an ideal solution.|F|It lowers the solvent mole fraction and vapor pressure.
An ideal nonvolatile solute lowers the freezing point of a solution.|T|The dissolved particles shift the solid-liquid equilibrium.
Osmosis is solvent flow through a semipermeable membrane.|T|The membrane permits solvent passage more readily than passage of the relevant solute.
A colloid is necessarily a true molecular solution.|F|Colloids contain dispersed particles larger than ordinary dissolved molecules or ions.
A spontaneous process is always fast.|F|Spontaneity concerns thermodynamic direction; reaction rate depends on kinetic barriers.
At constant temperature and pressure, negative Gibbs energy change favors the forward process.|T|The process can lower the system’s Gibbs energy under those constraints.
Entropy can be interpreted in terms of the number of accessible microscopic arrangements.|T|More accessible microstates correspond to higher entropy in the statistical description.
The entropy of the universe decreases for a spontaneous process.|F|The combined system and surroundings have a positive total entropy change for an irreversible spontaneous process.
A negative enthalpy change guarantees spontaneity at every temperature.|F|The entropy contribution also matters through Gibbs energy.
Standard reaction entropy is found by summing product values minus reactant values with coefficients.|T|Stoichiometric amounts weight the tabulated standard molar entropies.
At equilibrium, the reaction Gibbs energy is zero.|T|There is no net thermodynamic drive for either direction at the actual composition.
A positive standard Gibbs energy means the forward reaction is impossible at every composition.|F|Actual Gibbs energy also depends on reaction quotient and can differ in sign from the standard value.
The third law assigns zero entropy to a perfect crystal at absolute zero.|T|The ideal perfectly ordered ground state has a single microscopic arrangement in this statement.
Chemical equilibrium is dynamic.|T|Forward and reverse reactions continue while their rates are equal.
At equilibrium, reactant and product concentrations must be equal.|F|They are constant in time but need not be equal to each other.
The equilibrium constant changes when temperature changes.|T|Its thermodynamic value depends on temperature for a specified reaction.
A catalyst changes a reaction’s equilibrium constant.|F|It changes the speed of reaching equilibrium, not the equilibrium composition at fixed temperature.
Pure solids are omitted from a conventional equilibrium-constant expression.|T|Their activities are treated as one in their standard pure state.
If Q is smaller than K, the reaction tends forward toward products.|T|The present composition has too few products relative to the equilibrium ratio.
Reversing a reaction replaces K with its reciprocal.|T|Products and reactants exchange roles in the equilibrium expression.
Multiplying all reaction coefficients by two leaves K unchanged.|F|The equilibrium expression is squared, so the new constant is K squared.
Removing a product can cause an equilibrium mixture to form more product.|T|The reaction shifts to oppose the imposed concentration change as it approaches equilibrium again.
A Brønsted–Lowry acid donates a proton.|T|Its conjugate base is the species remaining after that donation.
A Brønsted–Lowry base accepts a proton.|T|Its conjugate acid is formed by gaining that proton.
A strong acid is the same thing as a concentrated acid.|F|Strength concerns ionization tendency; concentration concerns amount per volume.
The conjugate base of a strong acid is usually a very weak base.|T|Strong proton donation corresponds to weak tendency of the conjugate base to take the proton back.
At 25 °C, neutral pure water has pH 7.|T|Equal hydronium and hydroxide activities correspond approximately to this value under ordinary conditions.
Neutral pH is exactly 7 at every temperature.|F|The water ion-product constant changes with temperature, changing the neutral pH.
A buffer usually contains a weak acid and its conjugate base, or a weak base and its conjugate acid.|T|The pair can consume modest additions of either acid or base.
A buffer prevents every pH change regardless of how much acid is added.|F|Its capacity is finite; large additions exhaust the buffering components.

At the half-equivalence point of a simple weak-acid/strong-base titration, pH equals pKa approximately.|T|Equal amounts of the conjugate pair make the logarithmic ratio term zero under the buffer approximation.
The solubility product describes an equilibrium involving a sparingly soluble ionic solid.|T|It relates activities of dissolved ions when the solid is present at equilibrium.
Adding a common ion often lowers the solubility of an ionic solid.|T|The equilibrium shifts toward the solid to accommodate the increased ion activity.
A precipitate is favored when the relevant ion activity product exceeds Ksp.|T|The supersaturated mixture can lower the ion product by forming solid.
Ksp equals molar solubility for every ionic compound.|F|Stoichiometric ion powers and coefficients relate the two quantities differently for different formulas.
Complex-ion formation can increase a metal salt’s apparent solubility.|T|Binding dissolved metal lowers its free-ion activity and can draw more solid into solution.
A ligand can donate an electron pair to a metal ion.|T|This forms a coordinate interaction in a complex ion.
Changing pH can affect the solubility of salts containing acid-base-active ions.|T|Protonation or deprotonation changes free-ion concentrations and shifts dissolution equilibrium.
Every salt becomes more soluble when any acid is added.|F|The effect depends on the ions, competing equilibria, and possible new precipitates.
Selective precipitation can separate ions with sufficiently different precipitation conditions.|T|Controlling ion concentrations can precipitate one species while leaving another mainly dissolved.
Oxidation occurs at the anode.|T|This naming convention holds for both galvanic and electrolytic cells.
Reduction occurs at the cathode.|T|The cathode is the electrode where electrons are consumed by the reduction reaction.
Electrons travel through the salt bridge of a typical galvanic cell.|F|Electrons travel through the external conductor; ions carry charge through the salt bridge.
A galvanic cell converts a spontaneous chemical change into electrical work.|T|The redox reaction drives charge flow through the external circuit.
An electrolytic cell requires external energy to drive its nonspontaneous reaction.|T|An applied power source forces the desired redox direction.
Multiplying a half-reaction’s coefficients multiplies its standard electrode potential.|F|Potential is intensive and does not scale with the amount of reaction.
The Nernst equation accounts for nonstandard composition in cell potential.|T|Reaction quotient adjusts the standard potential for actual activities.
A positive cell potential corresponds to negative reaction Gibbs energy for the stated cell reaction.|T|The relation is ΔG = −nFE, with positive electron count n and Faraday constant F.
Charge passed in electrolysis equals current times time for constant current.|T|This charge determines electron amount and, through stoichiometry, the material transformed.
A rate law must always use the balanced equation’s coefficients as its exponents.|F|Overall rate laws are determined experimentally unless a justified elementary-step interpretation applies.
A catalyst lowers the activation barrier for an alternative pathway.|T|It increases the rate without changing the reaction’s equilibrium thermodynamics.
Increasing temperature often increases reaction rate.|T|More reacting particles can cross the activation barrier and the rate constant typically increases.
A first-order reaction has a concentration-independent half-life.|T|Its half-life equals ln 2 divided by the first-order rate constant.
A zero-order reaction’s rate is proportional to reactant concentration.|F|Its rate is independent of that concentration in the zero-order regime.
Reaction order can be noninteger.|T|Empirical rate laws can have fractional or other noninteger exponents.
An intermediate is formed and later consumed within a mechanism.|T|It cancels from the net reaction and is distinct from a transition state.
A catalyst is consumed permanently in the net catalytic reaction.|F|It is regenerated by the full catalytic cycle.
The Arrhenius equation relates rate constant to temperature and activation energy.|T|It describes how the energetic barrier influences temperature dependence over its useful regime.
Main-group elements occupy the s and p blocks of the periodic table.|T|Their valence electron patterns organize many representative-element trends.
Alkali metals commonly form +1 ions.|T|Losing their single outer s electron gives a closed-shell-like configuration.
Alkaline-earth metals commonly form +2 ions.|T|Their two outer s electrons are often lost in ionic compounds.
Halogens commonly gain one electron to form −1 ions.|T|One added electron completes their valence shell in common ionic compounds.
All oxides are strongly basic.|F|Oxides can be basic, acidic, or amphoteric depending on composition and bonding.
An amphoteric substance can react as either an acid or a base.|T|Its behavior depends on the reacting partner and conditions.
A metalloid can have properties intermediate between typical metals and nonmetals.|T|This mixed behavior often includes useful semiconducting properties.
Noble gases can never form compounds.|F|Some heavier noble gases form compounds under suitable conditions.
Allotropes are different structural forms of the same element.|T|Their bonding arrangements can give different physical and chemical properties.
A coordination complex contains a central atom or ion bound to ligands.|T|Ligands supply donor sites that coordinate to the center.
Coordination number counts directly attached donor atoms.|T|A multidentate ligand can contribute more than one donor atom.
Every ligand is negatively charged.|F|Neutral molecules such as water and ammonia can also be ligands.
A chelating ligand binds through more than one donor site.|T|Multiple attachments can form rings with the metal center.
Coordination number always equals metal oxidation state.|F|Oxidation state is charge bookkeeping, while coordination number counts attached donors.
Transition-metal complexes can be colored because of electronic transitions.|T|Absorption can involve split d levels or charge-transfer transitions, depending on the complex.
Octahedral crystal fields split the five d orbitals into two energy groups.|T|Their orientations relative to the ligands produce different electrostatic interactions.
High-spin and low-spin arrangements can differ in the number of unpaired electrons.|T|The competition between splitting energy and pairing energy controls orbital occupation.
Geometric isomers have the same formula but different spatial arrangements of ligands.|T|Cis and trans arrangements are common examples when the coordination geometry permits them.
Nuclear reactions can change one element into another.|T|Changing proton count changes elemental identity.
Chemical reactions routinely change atomic nuclei into different elements.|F|Ordinary chemical reactions rearrange electrons and bonds rather than altering nuclei.
Alpha emission decreases mass number by four and atomic number by two.|T|The emitted helium nucleus removes two protons and two neutrons.
Beta-minus decay increases atomic number by one while keeping mass number unchanged.|T|A neutron converts to a proton while emitting an electron and an antineutrino.
Gamma emission changes the nucleus’s mass number by one.|F|It releases energy without changing the nucleon count.
A radioactive sample’s activity depends on how many undecayed nuclei remain.|T|Activity equals the decay constant times the remaining number of radioactive nuclei.
After three half-lives, the expected remaining fraction is one-eighth.|T|Three successive halvings give one-half cubed.
Radiometric dating requires knowledge of an appropriate decay relationship and sample assumptions.|T|Interpretation depends on the isotope system and whether the relevant material behaved as assumed.
Fusion and fission are the same nuclear process.|F|Fusion combines light nuclei; fission splits heavy nuclei.
Carbon commonly forms four covalent bonds in neutral organic structures.|T|Its valence arrangement supports four shared electron-pair bonds in common closed-shell structures.
Alkanes contain carbon-carbon double bonds by definition.|F|Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with only single carbon-carbon bonds.
An alkene contains a carbon-carbon double bond.|T|That functional feature changes reactivity and can restrict rotation.
Alcohols contain a hydroxyl group attached to a carbon framework.|T|The O–H group gives characteristic polarity and hydrogen-bonding behavior.
A carboxylic acid contains a carbonyl and hydroxyl bonded to the same carbon.|T|This combined carboxyl group has properties distinct from an ordinary alcohol.
Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different connectivity.|T|Their atom-to-atom bonding arrangements differ.
A polymer consists of many linked repeating units.|T|Large chains or networks are built from smaller building-block molecules.
All organic compounds contain only carbon and hydrogen.|F|Many contain oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur, halogens, or other elements.
The functional group often helps predict an organic compound’s characteristic reactions.|T|Local bonding patterns give recurring reactivity even in different carbon frameworks.
